slides.title: Will it hold?
points: Statics works out the forces on a part at rest; materials science says how the material responds.
Together they answer whether a bracket, beam or bolt will bend, break or wear out.

slides.title: Forces, stress, strength
points: Free-body diagrams: draw every force and moment; at rest they sum to zero.
Stress is force per area; strain is how much the material stretches.
Each material has a yield strength (where it starts to bend permanently) and an ultimate strength (where it breaks).
A safety factor divides the strength by the expected stress, leaving margin for the unknown.

slides.title: Strong, light, cheap
points: Stronger materials usually cost more or weigh more; aluminium versus steel is a classic trade.
Repeated loads cause fatigue failure far below the static strength.
Stress concentrates at sharp corners and holes; fillets spread it.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Hand calculations to sanity-check simulations.
Material datasheets and standards (ASTM, ISO).
Design reviews that ask about the worst-case load.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Describing parts exactly
points: CAD (SolidWorks, Fusion, Creo, CATIA) models parts and assemblies in 3D.
GD&T (geometric dimensioning and tolerancing) says on the drawing how much each feature may vary and still work.

slides.title: Datums and tolerances
points: Parametric models capture design intent, so changing one dimension updates the rest sensibly.
Datums are the reference features everything is measured from.
GD&T controls form (flatness), orientation (perpendicularity), location (position) and runout.
Tolerances should reflect function: tight only where it matters.

slides.title: Tight tolerances cost money
points: Every tighter tolerance raises machining and inspection cost.
Loose tolerances may let assemblies not fit.
Tolerance stack-up: small variations add up across an assembly.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Drawings reviewed with manufacturing before release.
Tolerance stack-up analysis for critical fits.
Revision control on every drawing.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Testing designs on the computer
points: Finite element analysis (FEA) splits a part into small elements and solves for stress, deflection, heat or vibration.
It finds problems before building prototypes.

slides.title: Mesh, loads, constraints
points: The mesh: smaller elements where stresses change quickly, larger elsewhere.
Loads and boundary conditions must match reality; wrong supports give wrong answers.
Check convergence: refine the mesh until results stop changing.
Validate against hand calculations or test data.

slides.title: Pretty pictures can lie
points: Colourful stress plots look convincing even when inputs are wrong.
Singularities (sharp corners, point loads) show unrealistically high stress.
Detailed models take long to solve; simplify where it doesn't matter.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: ANSYS, Abaqus or built-in CAD simulation.
Simulation reports listing assumptions.
Physical tests to confirm critical results.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: How parts actually get made
points: The process chosen (machining, moulding, casting, sheet metal, 3D printing) shapes the design, the cost and the lead time.
Designers who know processes design parts that are easy to make.

slides.title: Match process to volume and shape
points: CNC machining: precise, flexible, costly per part; good for prototypes and low volume.
Injection moulding: expensive tooling, very cheap per part; good for high volume plastics.
Sheet metal: bending and cutting flat stock; cheap for enclosures and brackets.
Additive (3D printing): complex shapes, quick changes, slower and pricier per part at volume.

slides.title: Tooling against per-part cost
points: A mould costs tens of thousands up front and pays back only at volume.
Changing a moulded design after tooling is slow and costly.
Surface finish and tolerances vary by process.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Quotes compared across processes at different volumes.
Prototypes machined or printed before tooling.
Supplier capability checked before design freeze.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Designing parts that are easy and cheap to make
points: Design for manufacture (DFM) and assembly (DFA) shape a design so it's simpler to make, assemble and inspect.
Most of a product's cost is decided in design.

slides.title: Fewer parts, simpler features
points: Reduce part count: combine parts, use snap fits instead of screws where sensible.
Follow process rules: draft angles and uniform walls for moulding, standard bend radii for sheet metal.
Standard fasteners and materials lower cost and risk.
Parts that can only assemble one way prevent mistakes (poka-yoke).

slides.title: Elegant against makeable
points: A clever shape that needs a five-axis machine costs far more.
Fewer parts can mean harder servicing; balance repairability.
Early supplier input finds problems cheaply.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: DFM reviews with suppliers before release.
Part-count and assembly-time estimates in design reviews.
Checklists per manufacturing process.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: How electricity flows through components
points: Circuit analysis predicts voltages and currents through resistors, capacitors, inductors and semiconductors.
Everything in electronics builds on it.

slides.title: Ohm, Kirchhoff, components
points: Ohm's law: V = I × R.
Kirchhoff: currents into a node sum to zero; voltages round a loop sum to zero.
Capacitors store charge and pass changing signals; inductors resist changes in current.
Diodes let current flow one way; transistors switch or amplify.

slides.title: Ideal against real
points: Real components have tolerances, temperature drift and parasitics.
Power dissipated as heat (P = V × I) limits component choices.
Simulation (SPICE) helps, but bench measurement decides.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Multimeters and oscilloscopes on the bench.
Datasheets checked for ratings and derating.
Simulation before building.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Turning a circuit into a board
points: PCB design takes a schematic and places components and routes copper traces on a board that can be manufactured.
Layout affects noise, heat and reliability as much as the schematic.

slides.title: Placement, routing, grounding
points: Place components by function and signal flow; keep sensitive analogue parts away from noisy switching parts.
Solid ground planes give low-impedance return paths.
Trace widths sized for current; high-speed signals need controlled impedance and short returns.
Decoupling capacitors placed right next to each chip's power pins.

slides.title: Layers, size, cost
points: More layers make routing easier and cost more.
Smaller boards cost less and are harder to route and cool.
Design rules from the fabricator must be followed.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: KiCad, Altium or Cadence tools.
Design rule checks before ordering.
Test points and debug headers on early boards.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Information as voltage over time
points: Signals carry information: audio, sensor readings, radio, data.
Signal processing filters, samples and transforms them.

slides.title: Frequency, sampling, filtering
points: Any signal can be seen as a mix of frequencies (Fourier).
Sampling must be at least twice the highest frequency present (Nyquist) to avoid aliasing.
Filters keep wanted frequencies and remove others: low-pass, high-pass, band-pass.
Noise and interference are reduced by filtering, shielding and good layout.

slides.title: Sharp filters cost something
points: Steeper filters need more components or computation and add delay.
Higher sample rates mean more data and power.
Analogue filtering before sampling prevents aliasing that software can't undo.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Anti-aliasing filters before ADCs.
Spectrum analysis to find noise sources.
Digital filters in firmware or DSP.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Converting and controlling power efficiently
points: Power electronics converts electricity from one form to another: AC to DC, one DC voltage to another, DC to AC for motors.
Efficiency and heat are the central concerns.

slides.title: Linear against switching
points: Linear regulators are simple and quiet but waste the voltage difference as heat.
Switching converters (buck, boost) switch rapidly and use inductors and capacitors, reaching 85–95 % efficiency.
MOSFETs are the usual switches; their losses come from switching and conduction.
Inverters drive motors with variable frequency.

slides.title: Efficiency against noise
points: Switching converters are efficient and make electrical noise; layout and filtering matter.
Higher switching frequency shrinks components and raises switching losses.
Thermal design (heatsinks, airflow) is part of the circuit design.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Efficiency curves measured across loads.
Thermal cameras on prototypes.
EMC testing for emissions.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Making things follow commands
points: Control systems measure something (speed, temperature, position) and adjust an output to keep it on target.
Most run on microcontrollers in a loop.

slides.title: Feedback and PID
points: Closed loop: measure, compare with the set point, correct, repeat.
A PID controller combines proportional (react to error), integral (remove steady offset) and derivative (damp fast changes) terms.
Tuning trades speed of response against overshoot and stability.
The loop must run at a steady, fast enough rate.

slides.title: Fast against stable
points: Aggressive tuning responds fast and may oscillate.
Integral wind-up: the integral grows while the output is saturated; limit it.
Sensor noise feeds into the derivative term; filter it.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Step-response tests to tune gains.
Fixed-rate timer interrupts for control loops.
Simulation (MATLAB/Simulink) before hardware.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A bracket cracks after months of vibration, though its static stress is well below the yield strength. What's the likely cause?
choices: Fatigue from repeated loading, worsened by a sharp corner concentrating stress
Temperature had no effect, so it's random
why: Cyclic loads cause cracks below static strength, starting at stress raisers.

newQuestions.stem: A drawing puts ±0.01 mm on every dimension, including a decorative edge. What's the problem?
choices: Needless cost: tight tolerances should apply only where function requires them
why: Tight tolerances everywhere make the part expensive to make and inspect.

newQuestions.stem: An FEA shows extreme stress exactly at a sharp internal corner, and it keeps rising as the mesh is refined. What's going on?
choices: A stress singularity from the idealised sharp corner; model the real fillet radius or judge it with care
The mesh is too coarse, so refine more
why: A perfectly sharp corner gives infinite theoretical stress; real parts have a radius.
Not necessarily; the number isn't physical.
Refining makes it grow without converging.
It's behaving as the maths says.

newQuestions.stem: You need 50 prototype housings next week, and 100,000 per year later. Which plan fits?
choices: 3D-print or machine the prototypes now; design for injection moulding for volume
why: Fast, tool-free methods for prototypes; tooling pays off at volume.
Tooling takes weeks and costs too much for 50.

newQuestions.stem: An injection-moulded part has vertical walls with no draft and thick and thin sections side by side. What will the moulder say?
choices: Add draft angles so it releases from the mould, and make wall thickness uniform to avoid sink marks and warping
why: Draft and uniform walls are basic moulding rules.

newQuestions.stem: A 1 kΩ resistor has 5 V across it. How much current flows, and how much power does it dissipate?
A microcontroller resets randomly. Its decoupling capacitors are placed 5 cm away from the power pins. What's a likely fix?
choices: Place decoupling capacitors right next to the power pins with short paths to ground
why: Long paths add inductance, so the capacitors can't supply fast current spikes.

newQuestions.stem: A signal contains content up to 10 kHz and is sampled at 12 kHz. What happens?
choices: Aliasing: frequencies above 6 kHz fold back as false lower frequencies; filter first or sample above 20 kHz
why: Sampling must exceed twice the highest frequency, or use an anti-aliasing filter.

newQuestions.stem: A linear regulator drops 24 V to 5 V at 1 A and overheats. Why, and what's the usual fix?
choices: It dissipates (24 − 5) × 1 = 19 W as heat; use a switching (buck) converter
The output voltage is too low
why: Linear regulators burn the voltage difference; a buck converter is far more efficient.
Some can; the heat is the problem.

newQuestions.stem: A temperature controller overshoots badly and oscillates around the set point. Which change usually helps first?
choices: Reduce the proportional gain (and add some derivative damping), retuning step by step
why: Lower gain and damping reduce overshoot and oscillation.
